extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP practitioners, policymakers, and legal scholars interested in the America Invents Act and prior-user rights
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the statutory standards, scope, timing, and exceptions governing the AIA's prior-user defense (§273) and related AIA provisions (e.g., supplemental examination, USPTO sanctions). Focused on how to establish and limit the defense under U.S. law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination mandate (§257)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director 'shall' conduct supplemental examination and 'shall' address each substantial new question of patentability that is raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language is mandatory (use of 'shall'); the Director's regulatory authority under §257(d) is limited. Representative Waxman’s concerns (that supplemental examination might be used to present information not available at original filing) are discussed, and the statute does not limit supplemental examination to only information existing at original filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to sanction misconduct in USPTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA broadly shifts responsibility for sanctioning misconduct in USPTO proceedings from the federal courts to the USPTO itself (see Leahy‑Smith AIA secs. 6(a) §316(a)(6) and 6(d) §326(a)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative materials (House report) state the Director 'may impose sanctions in the form of monetary fines (or payments to other parties) or restrictive orders relating to the proceedings, including dismissal of petitions or cancellation of claims.' The shift to USPTO adjudication of misconduct is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of prior-user defense (applies to utility patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA added a prior-user defense that applies to all utility patents and can be asserted for any process or for any product that is used in a manufacturing or other commercial process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is broader than pre-AIA §273 (which had been limited to business-methods in some incarnations). The legislative history contrasts earlier, narrower (business-method-only) formulations with the eventual broader coverage under the AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter limitation: process or tangible things used in manufacturing/commercial process
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 273(a) limits the defense to subject matter 'consisting of a process, or consisting of a machine, manufacture, or composition of matter used in a manufacturing or other commercial process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee commentary notes that the 'process or method' limitation effectively precludes assertion of the defense for consumer products. Senator Leahy explained 'commercially used the subject matter' was intended to apply broadly across forms of subject matter that are embodied in processes or tangible things used in commercial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial-use requirement (§273(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person, acting in good faith, must have 'commercially used the subject matter in the United States, either in connection with an internal commercial use or an actual arm’s length sale or other arm’s length commercial transfer of a useful end result of such commercial use.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute requires use in the United States (earlier introduced bills had proposed allowing foreign uses, but the enacted provision requires U.S. commercial use). 'Commercially used' is interpreted broadly by supporters, but the text specifies internal commercial use or arm's-length sale/transfer of a useful end result as qualifying forms of commercial use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The person asserting the prior-user defense must be 'acting in good faith' when commercially using the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good faith is explicitly included in §273(a)(1) as a precondition to the defense; legislative materials emphasize it as part of the defendant’s burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / one-year limitation (§273(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial use must have occurred at least one year before the earlier of (A) the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or (B) the date on which the claimed invention was disclosed to the public in a manner that qualified for the exception from prior art under section 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ties the prior-user right to the §102(b) grace-period concept; the defendant must demonstrate the required commercial use timeline relative to filing or qualifying public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective-date/patent-issuance cutoff
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior-user defense can only be asserted against patents that are issued on or after September 16, 2011.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits retroactivity—patents issued before that date are not vulnerable to the §273 defense. The text notes that earlier, narrower statutory versions were seldom used.

rubrics_metrics.name: University-made invention exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The defense cannot be asserted against a patent for an invention that was made by a university (see Leahy‑Smith AIA, sec. 5(a), §273(e)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was included to address concerns from universities and tech-transfer stakeholders that broad prior-user rights would harm university licensing and discourage disclosure; legislative history emphasizes this carve-out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may assert the defense ('performed or directed the performance')
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute allows assertion by the person who 'performed or directed the performance' of the acts necessary to establish the defense (the House-report language had earlier used 'performed or caused the performance').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative text was amended on the floor to change who may assert the defense; commentators and reports discuss the variation (performed/caused vs. performed/directed) and the practical impact on who can plead the defense. Some legislative materials also note clarifications about 'affiliates' in earlier reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with §282(b) (affirmative defense framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 273 provides that 'a person shall be entitled to a defense under section 282(b)' with respect to qualifying subject matter—i.e., the prior-user right functions as an affirmative defense to infringement claims under §282(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, the defense must be pleaded/established as part of the accused infringer's defense under §282(b); legislative history discusses how it fits into infringement litigation posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliates' ability to assert the defense (legislative report note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative reports (e.g., the 2007 Senate Committee Report) discussed amendments to clarify that 'affiliates' of a user may also assert the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although treatment of affiliates varied across drafts and reports, the legislative history contains explicit discussion about whether and how affiliate entities can invoke prior-user rights; check the enacted text and notes for the exact scope in practice.
